item.title: Features
item.description:
Source: https://www.pgbouncer.org/features.html

  • Connection pooling modes with different connection reuse intervals:

    Session pooling
    PgBouncer assigns a server connection to a client for its entire session. The connection returns to the pool when the client disconnects. This mode changes connection assignment least often and supports all PostgreSQL features.
    Transaction pooling
    PgBouncer assigns a server connection only during a transaction. The connection returns to the pool when the transaction ends. Some PostgreSQL session features cannot work in this mode. The application must avoid these features. See the table below.
    Statement pooling
    This mode changes connection assignment most often. It uses transaction pooling but disallows multi-statement transactions. It enforces client autocommit mode and mainly targets PL/Proxy.

  • Low memory use: 2 kB per connection by default. PgBouncer does not need to hold a complete packet at once.

  • Destination databases can be on different hosts. PgBouncer is not limited to one backend server.

  • Supports online reconfiguration for most settings.

  • Supports rolling restarts and upgrades using multiple processes with so_reuseport. The legacy online restart (-R) was removed in 1.26.0.

item.title: E-R Model of Infra Cluster
item.description:
The INFRA module is a management hub made of infrastructure nodes, rather than a traditional cluster. It provides core services for the deployment. Each node is an autonomous service unit that runs components such as Nginx, Grafana, and VictoriaMetrics. Together, these nodes provide observability and management for database clusters.

There are two core entities in Pigsty’s INFRA module:

  • Node: A server that runs infrastructure components. It can be a physical server, VM, container, or Pod.
  • Component: An infrastructure service on a node, such as Nginx, Grafana, or VictoriaMetrics.

INFRA nodes usually also serve as administration nodes, which form the Pigsty control plane.

item.title: Introduction
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/README.html

Patroni is a Python template for high availability (HA) PostgreSQL solutions. It started as a fork of Governor, a Compose project, and adds many features.

For additional background info, see:

  • PostgreSQL HA with Kubernetes and Patroni, talk by Josh Berkus at KubeCon 2016 (video)
  • Feb. 2016 Zalando Tech blog post

Development Status

Patroni is in active development and accepts contributions. See Contributing for details.

See release information for new releases.

item.title: RPO Trade-offs
item.description:
RPO (Recovery Point Objective) defines the maximum amount of data loss allowed when the primary fails.

Critical data, such as financial transactions, typically requires RPO = 0: no data loss.

Stricter RPO targets increase write latency and reduce throughput. Replica failure can also make the primary unavailable. Some workloads accept limited data loss for higher performance and availability.

Trade-offs

Asynchronous replicas normally lag behind the primary by about 10KB–100KB or 100µs–10ms, depending on network and throughput. At primary failure, a replica might not have received the latest data. Promotion can lose those unreplicated changes.

item.title: Introduction
item.description:
PIG is a command-line tool for installing and managing PostgreSQL and its extensions. It maps extension names to RPM or DEB packages and uses apt, dnf, or yum to install them.

The catalog contains 616 extension entries. PIG selects package names for your PostgreSQL major version, operating system, and CPU architecture. It also provides commands for source builds, local PostgreSQL operations, backups, and Pigsty administration.

What you can do

Task Command Reference
Find an extension and check package availability pig ext list, pig ext avail Extensions
Add PGDG and Pigsty repositories pig repo add pgsql -u Repositories
Install PostgreSQL 18 and pgvector pig install -v 18 pg18 vector Getting started
Build an extension package from source pig build pkg NAME Build
Start, inspect, or stop a local PostgreSQL instance pig pg PostgreSQL
Manage a Patroni cluster pig pt Patroni
Back up or restore an instance pig pb, pig pitr pgBackRest, PITR
Configure Pigsty and run its playbooks pig sty, pig inventory, pig do Pigsty

Start with the tutorial to install PostgreSQL and enable your first extension.

item.title: E-R Model of PostgreSQL Cluster
item.description:
PGSQL organizes PostgreSQL as clusters. Each cluster is a logical group of database instances connected through primary-replica relationships.

Each cluster is an autonomous business unit with at least one primary instance. It exposes database capabilities through services.

There are four core entities in Pigsty’s PGSQL module:

  • Cluster: An autonomous PostgreSQL business unit and the top-level namespace for other entities.
  • Service: A named abstraction that exposes capabilities and routes traffic through node ports.
  • Instance: One PostgreSQL server, including its running processes and database files, on one node.
  • Node: A hardware resource that runs Linux and Systemd. It can be a physical server, VM, container, or Pod.

Two business entities, Database and Role, complete this logical model:

item.title: Failure Model
item.description:
Patroni failures have 10 categories by failure target. Detection paths group them into five categories, described here.

# Failure Scenario Description Final Path
1 PG process crash crash, OOM killed Active Detection
2 PG connection refused max_connections Active Detection
3 PG zombie Process alive but unresponsive Active Detection (timeout)
4 Patroni process crash kill -9, OOM Passive Detection
5 Patroni zombie Process alive but stuck Watchdog
6 Node down Power outage, hardware failure Passive Detection
7 Node zombie IO hang, CPU starvation Watchdog
8 Primary ↔ DCS network failure Firewall, switch failure Network Partition
9 Storage failure Disk failure, disk full, mount failure Active Detection or Watchdog
10 Manual switchover Switchover/Failover Manual Trigger

For RTO calculations, all failures follow two paths. This section calculates their minimum, maximum, and average recovery times.

item.title: E-R Model of Etcd Cluster
item.description:
The ETCD module organizes production ETCD into clusters. A cluster is a logical entity whose ETCD instances coordinate through the Raft consensus protocol.

Each cluster is an autonomous distributed key-value store with at least one ETCD instance. It provides services through client ports.

There are three core entities in Pigsty’s ETCD module:

  • Cluster: An autonomous ETCD service unit and the top-level namespace for other entities.
  • Instance: One ETCD server process on a node, participating in Raft consensus.
  • Node: An implicitly declared hardware resource that runs Linux and Systemd.

The ETCD model has no Service entities or complex Role distinctions, unlike PostgreSQL. All ETCD instances are functionally equivalent. Raft elects one Leader; the others become Followers. Non-voting Learner members are also permitted during intermediate scale-out states.

item.title: MINIO Cluster Model
item.description:
MINIO is the compatibility module name for object storage. Pigsty v4.5.0 deploys Silo with minio_type: silo. It groups object storage instances into a cluster.

Each cluster is an autonomous S3-compatible object store with at least one instance. It exposes services through the S3 API port.

There are three core entities in Pigsty’s MINIO module:

  • Cluster: An autonomous object storage service unit and the top-level namespace for other entities.
  • Instance: One Silo server process on a node, managing local disks.
  • Node: An implicitly declared hardware resource that runs Linux and Systemd.

Silo also retains the Storage Pool concept for expansion.

item.title: E-R Model of Redis Cluster
item.description:
The Redis module organizes production Redis into clusters. A cluster is a logical entity with Redis instances on one or more nodes.

Each cluster is an autonomous, high-performance cache or storage unit with at least one Redis instance. It exposes services through ports.

There are three core entities in Pigsty’s Redis module:

  • Cluster: An autonomous Redis service unit and the top-level namespace for other entities.
  • Instance: One Redis server process using a specific port on a node.
  • Node: An implicitly declared hardware resource that runs Linux and Systemd. It can host multiple Redis instances.

Redis usually runs multiple instances per node, unlike PostgreSQL. This uses multiple CPU cores on a physical server or VM. Nodes and instances therefore have a 1:N relationship. For production, Redis instances with more than 12 GB of memory are generally discouraged.

item.title: Replication modes
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/replication_modes.html

Patroni uses PostgreSQL streaming replication. See the Postgres documentation. Patroni configures asynchronous replication by default. Select a replication design for your business requirements. Compare asynchronous replication, synchronous replication, and other HA solutions before you select one.

Asynchronous mode durability

Asynchronous mode permits some committed transaction loss to maintain availability. If the primary fails or becomes unavailable, Patroni automatically promotes a sufficiently healthy standby. Transactions absent from that standby remain on a forked timeline on the old primary. They are effectively unrecoverable1.

item.title: Project Metrics
item.description:
Source: pgBackRest project metrics, captured for the 2.59.2 documentation snapshot.

Code Coverage

pgBackRest aims to have complete function/branch/line coverage for the core C code in /src.

Function/line coverage is complete with no exceptions.

Branch coverage excludes branches inside macros and assert() calls. Macros have separate unit tests, so each occurrence does not need testing. Asserts test conditions that should always be true and do not require complete branch coverage.

item.title: Watchdog support
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/watchdog.html

Multiple PostgreSQL primaries can lose transactions because their timelines diverge. This is called split-brain. Patroni must prevent PostgreSQL from accepting transaction commits after the leader key expires in the DCS. Normally, Patroni stops PostgreSQL if the leader lock update fails for any reason. This protection can fail for these reasons:

  • Patroni crashes because of a bug, insufficient memory, or an accidental kill by a system administrator.
  • PostgreSQL shutdown takes too long.
  • System load, a VM pause by the hypervisor, or other infrastructure problems prevent Patroni from running.

Patroni supports watchdog devices to guarantee correct behavior under these conditions. A software or hardware watchdog resets the whole system if it receives no keepalive heartbeat within a specified time. This adds protection if the usual Patroni split-brain controls fail.

item.title: DCS Failsafe Mode
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/dcs_failsafe_mode.html

The problem

Patroni uses the Distributed Configuration Store (DCS) for leader elections and network partition detection. A node can run Postgres as primary only if it can update the DCS leader lock. If the update fails, Patroni immediately demotes Postgres and starts it read-only. Failure frequency depends on the DCS. It is close to zero with Etcd dedicated to Patroni, but can be higher with the Etcd-backed K8s API.

item.title: Citus support
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/citus.html

Patroni automates deployment of Multi-Node Citus clusters.

TL;DR

Apply these rules:

  1. Install the Citus PostgreSQL extension on every node. The minimum supported version is 10.0. We recommend at least 11.2 for transparent worker switchovers and restarts.
  2. Use the same cluster name (scope) on all Citus nodes.
  3. Use the same superuser credentials on the coordinator and all workers. Configure pg_hba.conf to permit superuser access between all nodes.
  4. Permit worker access to the coordinator REST API. Use the same credentials. If client certificates are configured, the coordinator must accept worker certificates.
  5. Add this section to patroni.yaml:
citus:
 group: X  # 0 for coordinator and 1, 2, 3, etc for workers
 database: citus  # must be the same on all nodes

item.title: Integration with other tools
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tools_integration.html

Patroni can integrate with other tools in your stack. These examples show possible integrations. The list is not complete.

Barman

Patroni provides patroni_barman. This application communicates with pg-backup-api to run Barman operations remotely.

The application has two subcommands: recover and config-switch.

patroni_barman recover

Use the recover subcommand as a custom bootstrap method or replica creation method. See replica_imaging_and_bootstrap for details.

item.title: Architecture
item.description:
Pigsty uses a modular architecture and declarative interface. Combine modules to meet your requirements.

  • Use one or more modules from the modular design.
  • Describe the environment with a configuration inventory and parameters. Apply it with Ansible playbooks.
  • Run Pigsty on physical or virtual nodes with a compatible OS.

Modules

Pigsty uses a modular design with six main default modules: PGSQL, INFRA, NODE, ETCD, REDIS, and MINIO.

  • PGSQL: Self-healing HA Postgres clusters powered by Patroni, Pgbouncer, HAproxy, PgBackrest, and more.
  • INFRA: Local software repo, Nginx, Grafana, Victoria, AlertManager, Blackbox Exporter—the complete observability stack.
  • NODE: Tune nodes to desired state—hostname, timezone, NTP, ssh, sudo, haproxy, docker, vector, keepalived.
  • ETCD: Distributed key-value store as DCS for HA Postgres clusters: consensus leader election/config management/service discovery.
  • REDIS: Redis servers supporting standalone primary-replica, sentinel, and cluster modes with full monitoring.
  • MINIO: S3-compatible simple object storage that can serve as an optional backup destination for PG databases.

Combine modules through declarative configuration. For host monitoring, install INFRA on infrastructure nodes and NODE on managed nodes. Install ETCD and PGSQL across multiple nodes to form an HA PostgreSQL cluster automatically. You can reuse Pigsty infrastructure for custom modules; see REDIS and MINIO as examples. Compatibility modes, such as PostgreSQL Mongo mode, combine standard PGSQL and Docker APP workflows.

item.title: Security Considerations
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/security.html

Protect two Patroni cluster interfaces from unauthorized access: the distributed configuration storage (DCS) and the Patroni REST API.

Protecting DCS

Patroni and patronictl store data in the DCS and retrieve data from it.

The DCS contains no sensitive information, but it permits changes to some Patroni/Postgres settings. Protect the DCS first.

Protection depends on the DCS type. See settings for authentication and encryption parameters: tokens, basic authentication, and client certificates.

item.title: Nodes
item.description:
A node represents hardware resources and an operating system. It can be a physical server, virtual machine, container, or pod.

A node needs a Linux OS, systemd, and standard CPU, memory, disk, and network resources.

Install modules on nodes. The installed modules determine the node type:

Type Description
Regular Node A node managed by Pigsty
ADMIN Node The node that runs Ansible to issue management commands
INFRA Node Nodes with the INFRA module installed
ETCD Node Nodes with the ETCD module for DCS
MINIO Node Nodes with the MINIO module for object storage
PGSQL Node Nodes with the PGSQL module installed
… Nodes with other modules…

In a single-node deployment, one node has all roles: regular, administration, infrastructure, ETCD, and database.

item.title: ER Model
item.description:
A deployment is the largest entity in Pigsty. This entity-relationship diagram shows its main entities and their relationships:

A deployment is also an environment. Examples include Production (Prod), User Acceptance Testing (UAT), Staging, Testing, and Development (Devbox). Each environment has a Pigsty inventory that describes all its entities and attributes.

An environment usually has shared infrastructure (INFRA). This includes ETCD for the HA DCS and MINIO for centralized backup storage. Infrastructure serves multiple PostgreSQL clusters and other database modules. Deployments without infrastructure are also possible.

item.title: HA multi datacenter
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ha_multi_dc.html

A PostgreSQL cluster across multiple data centers uses replication for high availability. Replication can be synchronous or asynchronous. See replication modes.

Both modes require these considerations:

  • Postgres can run as primary or standby leader only if it owns and can update the leader key.
  • Use an odd number of etcd, ZooKeeper, or Consul nodes: 3 or 5.

Synchronous Replication

A multi-datacenter cluster needs at least 3 zones to tolerate a zone failure automatically.

item.title: Infra as Code
item.description:
Pigsty uses IaC and GitOps. Describe the environment in a declarative inventory. Apply it with idempotent playbooks.

Declare the target state with parameters. Playbooks can repeatedly adjust nodes to that state. This resembles Kubernetes CRDs and Operators, implemented through Ansible on physical servers and VMs.

Pigsty was designed to manage large PostgreSQL deployments. Its target was to reproduce more than 100 database clusters, PG/Redis services, and monitoring on prepared servers within ten minutes. Manual GUI operations cannot complete that work in the available time. CLI-based IaC provides precise, efficient control.

item.title: High Availability
item.description:
Overview

Pigsty PostgreSQL clusters include HA through Patroni, Etcd, and HAProxy.

A cluster with two or more instances gains automatic HA without extra configuration. A surviving instance can provide the complete database service. Clients can connect through any cluster node without tracking primary-replica changes.

Default norm mode targets RTO below 45 seconds. With asynchronous replication, pg_rpo=1MiB limits sampled lag for failover candidates. It does not bound actual data loss. Strict synchronous mode with crit.yml gives acknowledged transactions RPO = 0 during failover. Configure these settings for your hardware and reliability requirements.

item.title: Infrastructure
item.description:
Production HA PostgreSQL needs monitoring, alerts, logs, time synchronization, DNS, and software repositories. The INFRA module provides these services. It is optional but strongly recommended.

Overview

The following single-node deployment diagram shows INFRA components on the right:

Component Type Description
Nginx Web Server Unified entry for WebUI, local repo, reverse proxy for internal services
Repo Software Repo APT/DNF repository with all RPM/DEB packages needed for deployment
Grafana Visualization Displays metrics, logs, and traces; hosts dashboards, reports, and custom data apps
VictoriaMetrics Time Series DB Scrapes all metrics, Prometheus API compatible, provides VMUI query interface
VictoriaLogs Log Platform Centralized log storage; all nodes run Vector by default, pushing logs here
VictoriaTraces Tracing Collects slow SQL, service traces, and other tracing data
VMAlert Eval Rule/Alert Evaluates alerting rules, pushes events to Alertmanager
AlertManager Alert Manager Aggregates alerts, dispatches notifications via email, Webhook, etc.
BlackboxExporter Blackbox Probe Probes reachability of IPs/VIPs/URLs
DNSMASQ DNS Service Provides DNS resolution for domains used within Pigsty [Optional]
Chronyd Time Sync Provides NTP time synchronization to ensure consistent time across nodes [Optional]
CA Certificate Issues encryption certificates within the environment
Ansible Orchestration Batch, declarative, agentless tool for managing large numbers of servers

item.title: PGSQL Arch
item.description:
PGSQL organizes PostgreSQL as clusters. Each cluster is a logical group of database instances connected through primary-replica relationships.

Overview

The PGSQL module combines these components for production HA clusters:

Component Type Description
postgres Database Open-source relational database engine for PGSQL
patroni HA Manages PostgreSQL, coordinates failover, leader election, config changes
pgbouncer Pool Lightweight connection pooling middleware, reduces overhead, adds flexibility
pgbackrest Backup Full/incremental backup and WAL archiving, supports local and object storage
pg_exporter Metrics Exports PostgreSQL monitoring metrics in a Prometheus-compatible format
pgbouncer_exporter Metrics Exports Pgbouncer connection pool metrics
pgbackrest_exporter Metrics Exports backup status metrics
vip-manager VIP Binds L2 VIP to current primary node for transparent failover [Optional]

Enable vip-manager when needed. PGSQL also uses components from other modules:

item.title: Point-in-Time Recovery — A Time Machine for PostgreSQL
item.description:
Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) can restore an earlier cluster state after accidental deletion of data, a table, or a database.

Pigsty enables PITR in its standard PostgreSQL configuration. This work once required specialist DBA knowledge.

Replication Is Not Backup

High availability can fail over to another instance after hardware failure. However, replication is not backup.

Streaming replication sends every primary change to replicas within milliseconds. This includes DELETE without WHERE or DROP TABLE against the wrong database. Failover handles machine failure. If the data is wrong, every replica can contain the same error.

item.title: RTO Trade-offs
item.description:
RTO (Recovery Time Objective) defines the maximum time required for the system to restore write capability when the primary fails.

Critical transaction systems typically need the shortest practical RTO, often below one minute.

Shorter RTO increases false failover risk. Network jitter can appear to be a failure. Cross-datacenter or cross-region deployments often allow 1–2 minutes to reduce this risk.

Trade-offs

pg_rto controls the failover unavailability limit. Presets fast, norm, safe, and wide support different network and deployment conditions. The default is norm, approximately 45 seconds.

item.title: How PITR Works
item.description:
A database is a state machine. WAL (Write-Ahead Log) records its changes in order. PostgreSQL writes each change to WAL before applying it to data files. Keep a physical snapshot and all later WAL to replay the database to a selected consistent state.

PITR combines three elements: a snapshot (base backup), history (WAL archive), and a target where replay stops.

Snapshot: Base Backup

A base backup is a physical snapshot of the whole PostgreSQL cluster. It provides the recovery starting point. Pigsty uses pgBackRest to manage three backup types:

item.title: PITR Architecture
item.description:
The PITR principle is simple, but implementation must address several constraints. WAL archiving must not block production writes. Object storage backups need encryption. Backup jobs must follow the primary after failover, and shared repositories must isolate clusters. Large numbers of small objects can also limit throughput.

Pigsty uses pgBackRest with production defaults that address these constraints. This page describes the engine, repository abstraction, archive path, scheduler, and execution on the current primary.

item.title: Configure
item.description:
The configure configuration wizard generates pigsty.yml for your current environment.

This script is optional. If you know how to configure Pigsty, edit pigsty.yml directly and skip the wizard.

Quick Start

Enter the Pigsty source directory and run ./configure to start the wizard. Without arguments, it uses the meta single-node template:

cd ~/pigsty
./configure # Interactive configuration wizard, auto-detect environment and generate config

The command starts with the selected template. It detects the current node IP address and region, then generates pigsty.yml for that environment.

item.title: Parameters
item.description:
Use inventory parameters to customize infrastructure settings and database configuration.

Parameter List

The current source and reference pages list 373 public parameters across 10 official modules. See Reference - Parameter List for the complete list. The native MySQL 8.4 pilot module has 13 additional public parameters. They are listed separately and excluded from this total.

Module Groups Params Description
PGSQL 9 124 PostgreSQL high-availability cluster configuration
INFRA 10 73 Software repositories and Victoria observability infrastructure
NODE 11 73 Node initialization, system tuning, and operations baseline
ETCD 2 13 ETCD cluster and removal protection parameters
MINIO 2 22 Silo deployment, observability, and removal parameters
REDIS 2 22 Redis/Valkey deployment and removal parameters
DOCKER 1 8 Docker engine parameters
JUICE 1 2 JuiceFS instance and cache parameters
VIBE 1 18 Code/Jupyter/Node.js/Claude/Codex configuration
KAFKA 2 18 Kafka deployment and removal-protection parameters

Parameter Form

Parameters are key-value pairs that describe entities. A key is a string. A value can be a boolean, string, number, array, or object.

item.title: PITR Tradeoffs
item.description:
Backups require storage, network traffic, and operational work. They determine how much data you can recover and how quickly service returns. More history usually requires more capacity. A shorter RTO usually requires newer backups and tested procedures.

A backup policy must define repository location, history retention, and backup frequency.

Where: Choose the Failure Domain

Repository location is the most important choice. It determines which disasters the backup can survive.

item.title: Declarative Recovery
item.description:
A backup must support recovery when an incident occurs. Traditional PITR requires connected manual steps: pause HA, stop PostgreSQL, prepare recovery settings, restore the backup, and replay WAL. Then validate the target, rebuild metadata, and start the cluster again.

Pigsty uses declarative configuration for recovery. Declare the recovery target. The tools stop the cluster, restore data, replay WAL, and return control to the operator.

Declare a Recovery Target

Set pg_pitr to describe the target. Run pgsql-pitr.yml to restore it. The most common form selects a specific time:

item.title: PITR Scenarios
item.description:
Decisions can consume much of the available incident response time. Pigsty automates recovery steps, but the operator must decide three things. Select the target, choose in-place or clone recovery, and define how to validate the result.

Read and rehearse this framework before an incident.

Decision Framework

Scenario Typical problem Recommended workflow Target
Accidental DML DELETE or UPDATE affects the wrong rows Clone, validate, then copy back data time / xid
Dropped table, schema, or database DROP or an incorrect migration Clone, validate, then copy back objects time / name
Defective release or batch corruption Software writes incorrect data for a period Clone and compare before choosing repair or cutover time / xid
Audit, investigation, or forensics Inspect historical state Clone and hold at the target for inspection time / lsn
Whole-cluster or site loss Hosts or storage are gone or encrypted Recover in place on replacement infrastructure default / time

Two principles apply throughout:

item.title: Conf Templates
item.description:
The inventory defines the deployment through declarative configuration. Customize its pigsty.yml file for your requirements.

New users can start with ready-to-use templates for common deployment scenarios.

Each template is a predefined pigsty.yml file with defaults for a specific scenario.

Select a template, then change it to meet your requirements.

Using Templates

The optional configure wizard generates an inventory from your environment and input, with suitable defaults.

Use ./configure -c <conf> to select a template. <conf> is relative to conf; the .yml suffix is optional.

item.title: Use CMDB as Config Inventory
item.description:
Use a PostgreSQL metabase as a dynamic configuration source instead of static YAML files.

Overview

A CMDB (Configuration Management Database) stores configuration in database tables.

By default, Pigsty uses static pigsty.yml as the Ansible inventory.

A static file is simple. Larger deployments can need finer control, concurrent editing, and external integration beyond one file’s practical limits.

Feature Static YAML File CMDB Metabase
Querying Manual search/grep SQL queries with any conditions, aggregation analysis
Versioning Depends on Git or manual backup Database transactions, audit logs, time-travel snapshots
Access Control File system permissions, coarse-grained PostgreSQL fine-grained access control
Concurrent Editing Requires file locking or merge conflicts Database transactions naturally support concurrency
External Integration Requires YAML parsing Standard SQL interface, easy integration with any language
Scalability Difficult to maintain when file becomes too large Scales to physical limits
Dynamic Generation Static file, changes require manual application Immediate effect, real-time configuration changes

The sample pg-meta.meta database baseline defines the CMDB schema.

item.title: Monitoring System
item.description:
The built-in monitoring system provides metrics, logs, and alerting. Logs and alerts also support audit and traceability. It can monitor Pigsty-managed clusters, existing PostgreSQL clusters, and external RDS services.

Monitoring Targets

Pigsty monitoring covers these core targets:

  • PostgreSQL clusters and instances (SQL performance, connections, replication, transactions, checkpoints, WAL)
  • Infrastructure components (Grafana, VictoriaMetrics, Alertmanager, Nginx, etc.)
  • Host nodes (CPU, memory, disk, network, kernel)
  • Key middleware (ETCD, MINIO, REDIS, JUICE, VIBE, etc.)

Technology Stack

Component Purpose
Grafana Visualization dashboards, unified entry point, alert views
VictoriaMetrics Time-series metric ingestion, storage, and query
VictoriaLogs Structured log ingestion, indexing, and search
VMAlert + Alertmanager Alert rule evaluation and notification delivery
Exporter / Agent Database/system metric exposure and log forwarding

Onboarding Modes

Pigsty supports three ways to add monitoring:

item.title: Service Access
item.description:
Split read and write operations, route traffic correctly, and deliver PostgreSQL cluster capabilities reliably.

A service exposes database cluster capabilities through a stable interface that hides the underlying cluster details.

Services provide stable production access, especially during HA failover. Personal users usually do not need this abstraction.

Personal Users

Services are mainly for production. Personal users with one node can connect directly through the instance name or IP address.

item.title: Security and Compliance
item.description:
Databases usually store the most valuable and sensitive data in an information system. Attacks and failures can therefore have severe consequences. Security requires multiple controls: who can connect, what they can do, and whether traffic is protected. It must also record operations and support recovery of damaged, lost, or deleted data.

Pigsty provides a default security baseline through declarative configuration. Declare HBA rules, roles and privileges, certificates, encryption, backups, and audit policies as parameters in the inventory. Idempotent playbooks render and apply these settings.

item.title: Security Model
item.description:
Identify the root of trust and defensive layers before selecting security features. The root of trust needs the strongest protection. Multiple layers preserve some protection if one fails.

Trust Boundaries

Pigsty uses Ansible for declarative deployment. Its administration node is the control plane and needs the strongest protection.

Role Assets and Privileges
Admin node The pigsty.yml inventory, which normally contains system and application credentials; the CA private key; SSH administration access to every node
INFRA nodes Monitoring and alerts, DNS, Nginx ingress, and software repositories
Database nodes Database instances, local dbsu, and restricted sudo
Clients Database credentials or client certificates; access through service ports, HBA, and authentication

These roles have different capabilities, not a simple hierarchy. Protect these three assets in particular:

item.title: Authentication
item.description:
pg_hba.conf defines PostgreSQL Host-Based Authentication. It controls who can connect, the source address, the database, and the required identity check.

Manual HBA maintenance across a cluster requires care. Primary and replica rules can differ, and each instance stores its configuration in its data directory. Without a shared declaration and refresh process, instance rules can diverge.

Pigsty declares HBA rules in the inventory through declarative configuration. Playbooks render and distribute them consistently.

item.title: Access Control
item.description:
Authentication verifies identity. Authorization determines what that identity can do.

PostgreSQL GRANT and REVOKE provide precise control. Privilege problems usually arise from missing default conventions. Examples include making an application account the owner, retaining temporary superuser access after troubleshooting, and omitting grants on new tables.

Pigsty provides four role tiers, default privileges, and database isolation. This starting model reduces manual grants per database. Operators must still assign roles to match business boundaries and regularly review effective privileges.

item.title: Encrypted Communication
item.description:
TLS can provide transport encryption, server authentication, and client authentication. Configure each protection separately. Enabling server TLS does not make clients verify the server or make the server require client certificates.

Most TLS operational work involves certificate issuance, distribution, trust, and rotation. Without central management, services often skip verification or keep plaintext connections.

Pigsty manages PKI declaratively. Deployment creates a local self-signed CA, issues component certificates, and distributes trust. TLS is then ready for use.

item.title: Data Security
item.description:
Network boundaries, authentication, and access control reduce incident risk. Data controls must limit damage and support recovery after hardware failure, leaked credentials, or operator errors.

Data security must provide integrity, recoverability, confidentiality if copied, and records of what happened.

Integrity

Bad disk sectors, memory bit flips, and firmware defects can cause silent data corruption, with no immediate error. Pigsty enables pg_checksum: true by default. Initialization uses data-checksums. PostgreSQL calculates each page checksum on write and checks it on read.

item.title: Compliance
item.description:
Compliance requires continuous evidence of three elements:

  • Configuration: Security controls must be enabled. Pigsty directly provides configuration.
  • Process: The organization must establish access approval, change management, recovery exercises, and related procedures.
  • Evidence: Records must show that configuration and processes remain effective. The inventory, runtime logs, and monitoring system provide part of this evidence.

This page provides a pre-launch checklist and maps Pigsty capabilities to common compliance frameworks. These mappings support architecture and gap analysis. They are not an MLPS assessment, SOC 2 audit opinion, or legal advice.

item.title: Concepts
item.description:
Pigsty is a portable, extensible, open-source PostgreSQL distribution. It uses declarative configuration and automation to build production database services in local environments. Its tools, scripts, and operating practices support PostgreSQL services at enterprise RDS levels.

Pigsty means PostgreSQL In Great STYle. It also means Postgres, Infras, Graphics, Service, Toolbox, it’s all Yours. It provides self-hosted PostgreSQL with graphical monitoring. Find source code on GitHub and information in the official documentation. Try the Web UI in the online demo.

item.title: PostgreSQL Mongo Mode
item.description:
The mongo configuration template is a PostgreSQL deployment mode, not an independent Pigsty module. It combines:

  • PostgreSQL 18 managed by the standard PGSQL module
  • The documentdb extension and its required preload libraries
  • A stateless FerretDB proxy deployed with Pigsty’s Docker APP workflow

PostgreSQL manages all data, high availability, backups, monitoring, and the database lifecycle. FerretDB provides only the MongoDB wire-compatible endpoint.

Quick Start

The default template is a single-node deployment on 10.10.10.10. FerretDB listens on loopback by default.

item.title: Backup Mechanism
item.description:
Pigsty’s backup and restore operations execute pgBackRest commands. For safe operation, understand the pgBackRest model and how Pigsty maps its orchestration parameters to native options.

Core pgBackRest Concepts

Stanza: the Cluster’s Backup Identity

A stanza names one PostgreSQL backup configuration and isolates that cluster inside a repository. Pigsty uses pg_cluster as the stanza name. The pg-meta stanza stores data under backup/pg-meta/ and archive/pg-meta/. Thus, several clusters can share one repository.

item.title: HA Drill: Handling 2-of-3 Node Failure
item.description:
In a typical 3-node HA deployment, simultaneous failure of two nodes removes the majority. The system usually cannot complete automatic failover and needs manual intervention.

First, assess the two failed servers. If they can restart quickly, prioritize their recovery. Otherwise, use the Emergency Recovery Procedure.

The Emergency Recovery Procedure assumes that the administration node has failed and only one regular database node survives. In this case, the fastest recovery procedure is:

item.title: PostgreSQL
item.description:
PostgreSQL is a widely used open-source database.

Pigsty installs PostgreSQL 18 by default. It supports PostgreSQL 14 ~ 18 and provides 600 PG extensions.

Quick Start

Install Pigsty using the pgsql configuration template.

./configure -c pgsql # Use postgres kernel
./deploy.yml # Deploy the Pigsty core chain with native PostgreSQL

Most configuration templates use the PostgreSQL kernel by default. Examples include:

  • meta : Default, postgres with core extensions (vector, postgis, timescale)
  • rich : postgres with all extensions installed
  • slim : postgres only, no monitoring infrastructure
  • ha/full : 4-node sandbox for HA demonstration
  • pgsql : minimal postgres kernel configuration example

Configuration

The native PostgreSQL kernel requires no special configuration changes:

item.title: Supabase
item.description:
Supabase — Build in a weekend, Scale to millions

Supabase is an open-source Firebase alternative built on PostgreSQL. It provides authentication, ready-to-use APIs, edge functions, real-time subscriptions, object storage, and vector embeddings. The low-code backend platform can replace much of the backend development work. Database design and frontend knowledge can be sufficient to build a product.

Supabase’s motto is: “Build in a weekend, Scale to millions”. Its cloud service can be cost-effective for small deployments, such as 4c8g. For millions of users, consider self-hosting to meet functionality, performance, and cost requirements.

item.title: Deploy HA Citus Cluster
item.description:
Citus is a PostgreSQL extension that turns PostgreSQL into a distributed database. It scales horizontally across nodes to process large data volumes and query workloads.

Patroni v3.0+ provides native high-availability support for Citus. This simplifies Citus cluster setup. Pigsty also provides native support.

  • What is Citus
  • Patroni Citus Support

Note: Citus 13.x supports PostgreSQL 18, 17, 16, 15, and 14. Pigsty extension repo provides Citus ARM64 packages.

Citus Cluster

Pigsty natively supports Citus. The current complete configuration template is conf/ha/citus.yml.

item.title: Babelfish
item.description:
Babelfish is a PostgreSQL-based SQL Server compatibility layer, open-sourced by AWS.

Overview

Deploy Babelfish in mssql mode to add these features to PostgreSQL:

  • SQL Server wire protocol compatibility (TDS, 1433)
  • T-SQL compatibility
  • Unified integration with Pigsty capabilities (HA, backup, monitoring, IaC)

In Pigsty v4, Babelfish supports PostgreSQL 17/18. The default template uses pg_version: 17. Babelfish is part of Pigsty’s standard delivery process and supports all Linux platforms.

item.title: Percona
item.description:
Percona Postgres is a patched Postgres kernel with pg_tde (Transparent Data Encryption) extension.

From v4.4.0, Pigsty installs Percona PostgreSQL under the private prefix /usr/pgtde-$v. Version v4.5.0 keeps this layout, with /usr/pgtde-18 for PostgreSQL 18. The pgtde package alias installs both the kernel package and its contrib package. These packages include pg_tde, PostGIS, pgvector, wal2json, pg_repack, pgaudit, and pg_stat_monitor.

  • Performance Test for Percona Transparent Data Encryption (TDE)

Quick Start

Use Pigsty’s standard installation process with the pgtde configuration template.

item.title: openHalo
item.description:
OpenHalo is an open-source PostgreSQL kernel that provides MySQL wire-protocol compatibility.

openHalo is based on PostgreSQL 14.18 and provides wire-level compatibility with MySQL 5.7.32-log / 8.0. Pigsty delivers it through pg_mode: mysql and the openhalo package alias.

Pigsty supports OpenHalo deployment on all supported Linux platforms.

  • RPM build spec: github.com/pgsty/rpm/rpmbuild/specs/openhalodb.spec
  • DEB build spec: github.com/pgsty/deb/debbuild/openhalodb

Quick Start

Use Pigsty’s standard installation flow with the mysql template.

curl -fsSL https://repo.pigsty.io/get | bash; cd ~/pigsty;
./configure -c mysql # Use MySQL (openHalo) template
./deploy.yml # Install (change passwords in pigsty.yml before production use)

Cluster Config 

pg-meta:
 hosts:
 10.10.10.10: { pg_seq: 1, pg_role: primary }
 vars:
 pg_cluster: pg-meta
 pg_users:
 - {name: dbuser_meta ,password: DBUser.Meta ,pgbouncer: true ,roles: [dbrole_admin] ,comment: pigsty admin user }
 - {name: dbuser_view ,password: DBUser.Viewer ,pgbouncer: true ,roles: [dbrole_readonly] ,comment: read-only viewer for meta database }
 pg_databases:
 - {name: postgres, extensions: [ aux_mysql ]} # mysql-compatible database
 - {name: meta ,baseline: cmdb.sql ,comment: pigsty meta database ,schemas: [pigsty]}
 pg_hba_rules:
 - {user: dbuser_view , db: all ,addr: infra ,auth: pwd ,title: 'allow grafana dashboard access cmdb from infra nodes'}
 pg_crontab: [ '00 01 * * * /pg/bin/pg-backup full' ] # full backup at 1 AM daily

 # OpenHalo specific settings
 pg_mode: mysql
 pg_version: 14
 pg_packages: [ openhalo, pgsql-common ]

The OpenHalo extension aux_mysql provides functions and types for MySQL compatibility. Enable it in the postgres database for full compatibility behavior.

item.title: OrioleDB
item.description:
OrioleDB is a PostgreSQL storage engine extension. It claims to provide 4x OLTP performance and to eliminate xid wraparound and table bloat issues. It also claims to provide cloud-native storage, with data stored in S3.

Pigsty ships OrioleDB as a patched PostgreSQL kernel plus the OrioleDB extension.

You can run OrioleDB as an RDS with Pigsty. Current packages support PostgreSQL 16, 17, and 18 on supported Linux platforms. Set pg_mode to oriole to use the /usr/oriole-$v installation path. The orioledb package alias resolves to versioned kernel packages, such as orioledb-16, orioledb-17, and orioledb-18. The current Pigsty package line is OrioleDB 1.8 beta16.

item.title: Cloudberry
item.description:
Cloudberry is an open-source MPP data warehouse kernel derived from the Greenplum ecosystem. It supports large-scale parallel analytics workloads.

Overview

In Pigsty, Cloudberry uses gpsql mode and shares the same identity model, monitoring logic, and directory conventions as Greenplum / MatrixDB.

  • Kernel package: cloudberry
  • Mode identifier: pg_mode: gpsql
  • Role flag: gp_role: master | segment
  • Current repo version: Cloudberry 2.1.0
  • Current main package version: DEB 2.1.0-2PIGSTY, RPM 2.1.0-3PIGSTY
  • Default binary directory: /usr/cloudberry

Pigsty currently provides package delivery, node management, monitoring integration, access control, and configuration management for Cloudberry. For MPP cluster initialization, scale-out, rebalance, and other upstream operations, you should use the official Cloudberry tools.

item.title: AgensGraph
item.description:
AgensGraph is a property graph database kernel built on PostgreSQL. It supports openCypher queries and mixed Cypher/SQL workflows.

Overview

Pigsty integrates AgensGraph through pg_mode: agens while preserving most of the standard PostgreSQL operational model.

  • Kernel package: agensgraph
  • Mode identifier: pg_mode: agens
  • Current template version: AgensGraph 2.17.0
  • Current version string: PostgreSQL 17.10 (AgensGraph 2.17.0)
  • Built-in template: agens
  • Typical use cases: graph relationship analysis, path queries, knowledge graphs, and risk/association analysis layered onto relational data

AgensGraph uses the PostgreSQL wire protocol. Standard PostgreSQL clients, drivers, and connection pools can connect directly. AgensGraph adds graph objects, Cypher syntax, and the agtype data type to the database.

item.title: pgEdge
item.description:
pgEdge is a distributed PostgreSQL distribution for edge deployments. It uses Spock multi-master logical replication.

Overview

Pigsty integrates pgEdge through pg_mode: pgedge and delivers it through the standard PostgreSQL cluster workflow:

  • pgedge: a PG15, PG16, PG17, and PG18 compatible kernel; the template defaults to PG18
  • spock: Active-active multi-master logical replication
  • snowflake: Distributed unique sequences
  • lolor: Large object logical replication compatibility layer

The current Pigsty repository supplies the versioned kernel packages pgedge-15, pgedge-16, pgedge-17, and pgedge-18. The template defaults to pg_version: 18. The pgedge-$v kernel package includes the control files, SQL files, and shared libraries for spock, snowflake, and lolor. Thus, these extensions are no longer separate packages in pg_extensions. pgEdge supports the PostgreSQL wire protocol, so psql, JDBC/ODBC, DBeaver, and similar tools work as usual.

item.title: DocumentDB
item.description:
Microsoft maintains DocumentDB, an open-source PostgreSQL document database extension. FerretDB is a stateless protocol translation proxy built on DocumentDB. Together, they provide a MongoDB wire-compatible endpoint for a standard PostgreSQL kernel. Applications can connect directly with MongoDB drivers. FerretDB translates their requests into PostgreSQL operations.

This stack is not a standalone PostgreSQL fork. The data layer uses native PostgreSQL 16–18, which the standard PGSQL module manages. PostgreSQL provides persistence, transactions, high availability, backup, monitoring, and access control. FerretDB runs as a Pigsty Docker APP and handles only protocol translation.

item.title: PG Kernels
item.description:
In Pigsty, you can replace the native PostgreSQL kernel with a variant that provides specialized features.

Pigsty supports multiple PostgreSQL kernels and compatibility branches within one operational framework. These kernels provide compatibility layers, multi-master replication, graph queries, MPP warehousing, transparent encryption, and other features.

The level of Pigsty integration differs between kernels. PostgreSQL, Citus, Babelfish, IvorySQL, PolarDB, AgensGraph, and pgEdge have defined templates and configuration procedures. Cloudberry and Greenplum usually use gpsql mode. For their MPP initialization and scale-out operations, upstream tools remain the preferred method.

item.title: Citus
item.description:
Pigsty natively supports Citus. This is a distributed horizontal scaling extension based on the native PostgreSQL kernel.

Installation

Citus is a PostgreSQL extension plugin. Use the standard extension installation procedure to install and enable it on a native PostgreSQL cluster.

./pgsql.yml -t pg_extension -e '{"pg_extensions":["citus"]}'

Configuration

To define a Citus cluster, set these parameters:

  • pg_mode must be set to citus instead of the default pgsql
  • You must define the shard name pg_shard and shard number pg_group on each shard cluster
  • You must define pg_primary_db to specify the database managed by Patroni
  • You can run administration commands as postgres from pg_dbsu, instead of the default pg_admin_username. If you use this account, you must set pg_dbsu_password to a non-empty plaintext password.

You also need HBA rules that allow SSL access from localhost and other data nodes.

item.title: IvorySQL
item.description:
IvorySQL is an open-source PostgreSQL kernel fork that aims to provide Oracle compatibility.

Overview

The Pigsty PGSQL repository provides IvorySQL 5.4 packages compatible with PostgreSQL 18.4. Packages cover the currently supported EL, Debian, and Ubuntu platforms on both architectures. Online installation uses Pigsty’s pgsql repository. The Professional Edition also provides offline delivery for these platforms.

Pigsty’s ivorysql package alias points to IvorySQL 5, which is compatible with PostgreSQL 18. Platform variables under roles/node_id/vars/ map the alias to package names. For example, EL uses ivorysql5, and Debian/Ubuntu uses ivorysql-5.

item.title: PolarDB PG
item.description:
Overview

Use Pigsty and PolarDB to create PostgreSQL clusters with “domestic innovation qualification” credentials.

PolarDB for PostgreSQL now uses PostgreSQL 17 as its base. The Pigsty polar template, default path, and extension notes now use PG17. Any client tool that supports the PostgreSQL wire protocol can connect to PolarDB clusters.

Pigsty’s PGSQL repository provides PolarDB PG open-source installation packages. Pigsty does not download these packages to the local software repository during installation.

item.title: PolarDB Oracle
item.description:
Use Pigsty to create PolarDB for Oracle clusters with “domestic innovation qualification” credentials.

The Security and Reliability Evaluation Results Announcement (No. 1, 2023) lists PolarDB v2.0 in Appendix 3, Centralized Database. It identifies PolarDB v2.0 as an autonomous, controllable, secure, and reliable domestic innovation database.

PolarDB for Oracle is an Oracle-compatible version based on PolarDB for PostgreSQL. Both use the same kernel. The --compatibility-mode parameter selects the mode.

We work with the Alibaba Cloud kernel team to provide a complete database solution with the PolarDB v2.0 kernel and Pigsty. For inquiries, contact sales. You can also purchase it on Alibaba Cloud Marketplace.

item.title: Greenplum
item.description:
Pigsty supports deployment of Greenplum clusters and the derivative distribution YMatrixDB. You can also add existing Greenplum deployments to Pigsty monitoring.

Overview

Only the professional/enterprise editions provide Greenplum / YMatrix cluster deployment. This capability is not currently open source.

Installation

Pigsty provides installation packages for Greenplum 6 (@el7) and Greenplum 7 (@el8). Open-source users can install and configure them manually.

item.title: Patroni 4.1.5 Documentation
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/index.html

Warning

Running Patroni on memory-restricted systems with Python 3.11+

Unexpected behavior can occur with Python 3.11 or newer on systems with strict memory limits. For example, this includes vm.overcommit_memory=2, which is recommended for PostgreSQL. You may observe these symptoms:

  • Patroni appears healthy
  • PostgreSQL continues to run
  • Patroni REST API becomes unresponsive
  • The operating system reports that Patroni is listening on the REST API port
  • Patroni logs look normal; however, following messages may appear once: Exception ignored in thread started by: <object repr() failed>, MemoryError
  • Kernel logs may contain messages such as not enough memory for the allocation

A bug in Python 3.11+ causes this behavior. Under strict memory conditions, a new thread may hang indefinitely if free memory is insufficient.

item.title: PgBouncer 1.26.0 Documentation
item.description:
Source: https://www.pgbouncer.org/

This manual is based on PgBouncer 1.26.0, released on 2026-09-23. See the release notes for the changes from earlier versions.

pgbouncer is a PostgreSQL connection pooler. Applications connect to pgbouncer as they would to a PostgreSQL server. pgbouncer creates a server connection or reuses an existing connection.

pgbouncer reduces the performance cost of opening new PostgreSQL connections.

To preserve transaction semantics, pgbouncer supports these connection pooling modes:

  • Session pooling: PgBouncer assigns a server connection to a client for its entire session. When the client disconnects, the connection returns to the pool. This is the default mode and changes connection assignment least often.
  • Transaction pooling: PgBouncer assigns a server connection only during a transaction. When the transaction ends, the connection returns to the pool.
  • Statement pooling: The connection returns to the pool immediately after each query. This mode changes connection assignment most often and does not allow multi-statement transactions.
